title: JOB SCHEDULER
subtitle: Ten thousand jobs per second, each within two seconds of its scheduled time.
footer: DDIA: Ch 9 leader election · Ch 8 leases / fencing · Ch 6 time partitioning   ·   Similar: Payment system · Online judge

items: Cron on one machine is a single point of failure that can't scale.
Store executions partitioned by time; a poller moves soon-due jobs into a delay queue that releases each on time.
Workers lease jobs with a visibility timeout, so crashed jobs are retried; jobs must be idempotent.
Schedule jobs: one-off at time T, or cron
Execute jobs with a retry policy
View job status and history
10k job executions/s
Start within 2s of scheduled time
At-least-once; jobs idempotent
Never lose a job; billions of jobs stored
10k executions/s = 864M/day.
A DB poll every second for "due now" across billions of rows will not hold, so use a two-layer design.

Naive: cron on one server. A single point of failure that can't scale.

items: Store executions in a DB partitioned by time bucket; a poller fetches executions due in the next few minutes.
Two layers: the poller hands near-due jobs to a delay queue that releases each one at its exact time, giving second-level precision without hammering the DB.
Workers take jobs with a visibility timeout (lease). A crash means the job reappears and is retried, so jobs must be idempotent.
How do you hit 2s precision?
DB scan every few minutes → delay queue (SQS DelaySeconds ≤ 15 min, or a Redis ZSET by timestamp) releases on time.
Worker dies mid-job?
Lease expires and the job is retried. Heartbeats extend leases for long jobs; fencing token on completion writes.
Duplicate enqueues?
Dedupe by execution_id at the queue or worker.
User history queries?
Secondary index on (user_id, scheduled_at).
Polling the entire jobs table every second.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
